title: Discrete Gauss-Bonnet: Curvature to Euler Characteristic
description: Proves the discrete Gauss-Bonnet theorem connecting angular deficiency to topology: the total angular deficiency at vertices of a polyhedral surface equals 2πχ, where χ is the Euler characteristic. Includes Descartes' theorem for convex polyhedra (4π), genus generalization, curvature-topology correspondence, all five Platonic solid computations, and the classification of regular polyhedra. 37+ theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Descartes discovered around 1630 that the total angular deficiency of a convex polyhedron equals 4π, though his work remained unpublished until 1860. Euler established V - E + F = 2 in 1758. Gauss (1827) and Bonnet (1848) developed the continuous version relating Gaussian curvature to topology: the Gauss-Bonnet theorem ∫∫ K dA = 2πχ. For polyhedral surfaces, curvature concentrates at vertices as angular deficiency, and the integral becomes a sum. The theorem was extended to all closed surfaces by von Dyck (1888) and to abstract Riemannian manifolds by Chern (1944-1945) using characteristic classes, making it a cornerstone of modern differential topology.
overview.problemStatement:
**Theorem (Discrete Gauss-Bonnet)**: For a polyhedral surface with angular deficiency δ(v) = 2π − (sum of face angles at v) at each vertex v:

$$\sum_v \delta(v) = 2\pi \chi$$

where χ = V − E + F is the Euler characteristic. For convex polyhedra (χ = 2), this gives Descartes' theorem: Σ δ(v) = 4π.
overview.text: Proves the discrete Gauss-Bonnet theorem connecting angular deficiency to topology: the total angular deficiency at vertices of a polyhedral surface equals 2πχ, where χ is the Euler characteristic. Includes Descartes' theorem for convex polyhedra (4π), genus generalization, curvature-topology correspondence, all five Platonic solid computations, and the classification of regular polyhedra. 37+ theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Algebraic proof by double-counting**:

1. Each face (p-gon) has interior angle sum (p−2)π
2. Double counting: Σ p_F = 2E, so total face angles = (2E−2F)π
3. Total deficiency: Σ δ(v) = 2πV − (2E−2F)π = 2π(V−E+F) = 2πχ

The proof is entirely combinatorial/algebraic — no differential geometry needed.
keyInsights: The discrete Gauss-Bonnet theorem is purely algebraic: it follows from double-counting face-edge incidences and the polygon angle sum formula
Total angular deficiency is a topological invariant: two surfaces with the same Euler characteristic have the same total deficiency, regardless of their geometric realization
The sign of total curvature determines the genus: positive → sphere (g=0), zero → torus (g=1), negative → higher genus (g≥2)
The Schläfli inequality 2p + 2q > pq from positive curvature limits regular polyhedra to exactly 5 types: {3,3}, {3,4}, {3,5}, {4,3}, {5,3}
For polyhedra, the continuous Gauss-Bonnet integral ∫∫ K dA reduces to the sum of vertex deficiencies because curvature is zero on faces and edges

sections.title: Polyhedral Surface with Angle Data
sections.summary: PART 1: The PolyhedralSurface structure carrying V, E, F counts, χ, the Euler relation V-E+F=χ, totalFaceAngleSum with the double-counting identity (2E-2F)π, and totalDeficiency = 2πV - totalFaceAngleSum.

sections.title: Polygon Interior Angle Sum
sections.summary: PART 2: Interior angle sums (p-2)π for triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, and hexagon, established by ring.

sections.title: Double Counting Identity
sections.summary: PART 3: The double-counting rewrite total face angles = 2(E-F)π, the algebraic core linking face-angle data to E and F.

sections.title: The Discrete Gauss-Bonnet Theorem
sections.summary: PART 4: Main theorem discrete_gauss_bonnet (Σδ = 2πχ) via the deficiency and angle-sum identities, with corollaries descartes_total_deficiency (χ=2 ⟹ 4π) and torus_zero_deficiency (χ=0 ⟹ 0).

sections.title: Genus Generalization
sections.summary: PART 5: OrientableSurface with χ = 2-2g, gauss_bonnet_genus (Σδ = 2π(2-2g)), and the sphere/torus/double-torus deficiency values plus non-positive curvature for genus ≥ 2.

sections.title: Curvature Sign and Topology
sections.summary: PART 6: Sign of total deficiency determines χ (positive/nonneg/zero curvature ⟹ corresponding χ sign) and positive curvature ⟹ genus 0.

sections.title: Uniform Curvature (Regular Polyhedra)
sections.summary: PART 7: For uniform per-vertex curvature, each vertex carries deficiency 2πχ/V.

sections.title: Platonic Solid Angular Deficiencies
sections.summary: PART 8: Concrete PolyhedralSurface instances for all five Platonic solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron), each verified to satisfy Gauss-Bonnet with total deficiency 4π.

sections.title: Per-Vertex Deficiency Computations
sections.summary: PART 9: Per-vertex angular deficiencies for each Platonic solid (2π minus face-angle sum) and the V × deficiency = 4π consistency checks.

sections.title: Genus Bounds from Curvature
sections.summary: PART 10: Total deficiency determines genus via Σδ = 4π(1-g); positive ⟹ genus 0, zero ⟹ genus 1, negative ⟹ genus ≥ 2.

sections.title: Topological Invariance
sections.summary: PART 11: Equal Euler characteristic forces equal total deficiency, so face and edge subdivisions preserve total curvature.

sections.title: Toroidal and Higher-Genus Examples
sections.summary: PART 12: Explicit OrientableSurface instances for a minimal polyhedral torus (χ=0, Σδ=0) and a double torus (χ=-2, Σδ=-4π).

sections.title: Vertex Count Bounds
sections.summary: PART 13: For convex polyhedra (χ=2), a positive minimum deficiency bounds V ≤ 4π/δ_min, with average deficiency 4π/V and the bound ≤ π for V ≥ 4.

sections.title: Connection to Continuous Gauss-Bonnet
sections.summary: PART 14: The discrete curvature measure equals 2πχ and all curvature concentrates at vertices (face and edge curvature vanish).

sections.title: Regular Polyhedra Classification from Curvature
sections.summary: PART 15: The Schläfli constraint 2p+2q>pq for positive curvature yields exactly five regular polyhedra (p,q ≤ 5), with p≥6 or q≥6 ruled out; followed by the summary block.

conclusion.summary: The discrete Gauss-Bonnet theorem reveals that the total angular deficiency of a polyhedral surface is entirely determined by its topology (Euler characteristic), not its geometry. This algebraic proof demonstrates the deep connection between local curvature and global topology.

crossReferences.description: Extends Euler's formula V-E+F=2 (Wiedijk #25) by interpreting it as a special case of the discrete Gauss-Bonnet theorem: total angular deficiency Σδ(v) = 2πχ
The discrete Gauss-Bonnet theorem proved here is the combinatorial foundation for the smooth Gauss-Bonnet formalization (OQ-02-OQ-01), which extends it to Riemannian surfaces
OQ-01 develops graph-theoretic consequences of Euler's formula (coloring, planarity); this OQ-02 develops the geometric consequences (curvature, angular deficiency, Platonic solids)
